title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
subtitle: How two programs agree on secret keys, prove who they are, and then talk privately over an open network.
summary: TLS 1.3 provides a secure channel over any reliable byte stream, giving authentication, confidentiality and integrity against an attacker who controls the network. A one-round-trip handshake negotiates algorithms and derives keys, and a record protocol then protects the data with AEAD encryption. RFC 9846 is the July 2026 revision of TLS 1.3 and obsoletes RFC 8446 and the TLS 1.2 specification, RFC 5246, along with RFC 5077, 6961, 7627 and 8422.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS 1.3 provides a secure channel over any reliable byte stream, giving authentication, confidentiality and integrity even against an attacker who controls the network. A one-round-trip handshake negotiates algorithms and keys, and a record protocol then encrypts the data. RFC 9846 is the July 2026 revision of TLS 1.3 and obsoletes RFC 8446 and RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2), along with RFC 5077, 6961, 7627 and 8422.

tldr.problem: Applications that talk over the Internet need privacy, tamper detection and proof of who they are talking to, even when attackers control the network.
tldr.mechanism: A handshake exchanges key shares and signed or PSK-based proofs in one round trip, derives keys with HKDF, and then a record protocol protects every record with an AEAD cipher.
tldr.outcome: It is the current version of the protocol behind HTTPS and many other secure connections, with legacy ciphers and non-forward-secret key exchange removed.

today: TLS 1.3 is what browsers and servers negotiate for HTTPS whenever both sides support it, and RFC 9001 uses the TLS 1.3 handshake inside QUIC. Libraries such as OpenSSL, rustls and Go's crypto/tls implement it. Since this document keeps the same version number and is backward compatible with RFC 8446, existing TLS 1.3 deployments are expected to keep working.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) gives two programs a secure channel over an untrusted network. The only thing it asks of the layer below is a reliable, in-order byte stream, which in practice means TCP. The RFC lists three promises: authentication (the server is always authenticated, the client optionally), confidentiality (only the endpoints can read the data, though lengths are not hidden) and integrity (tampering is detected). These are meant to hold even against an attacker who controls the whole network.

TLS has two parts. The handshake protocol authenticates the peers, negotiates algorithms and produces shared keys. The record protocol then uses those keys to protect a stream of records. TLS says nothing about how an application decides to start a handshake or how to check the identity in a certificate; each application protocol has to specify that itself.

RFC 9846 is the July 2026 revision of TLS 1.3. It obsoletes RFC 8446, the original TLS 1.3 specification, and also obsoletes RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and RFCs 5077, 6961, 7627 and 8422, which pertain to TLS 1.2 or earlier. It keeps the same version number and is backward compatible with RFC 8446.

TLS 1.3 is identified on the wire in an unusual way. Both hellos carry legacy_version 0x0303 (the TLS 1.2 number), and the real version, 0x0304, is announced in the supported_versions extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport Layer Security (TLS) gives two programs a secure channel over an untrusted network, using any reliable, in-order byte stream such as TCP. It provides authentication (the server always, the client optionally), confidentiality (message lengths are not hidden) and integrity. The handshake protocol authenticates peers and produces keys, and the record protocol uses them to protect data.

sections.title: What Changed and Why
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 was a big redesign of TLS 1.2, and RFC 9846 refines that redesign. The main differences from TLS 1.2 are that every remaining cipher is an AEAD cipher, static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman key exchange are gone so all public-key exchanges give forward secrecy, and all handshake messages after the ServerHello are encrypted. A new key derivation design built on HKDF replaces the old one, and the ChangeCipherSpec message is dropped except for middlebox compatibility. Compression, DSA and custom DHE groups were removed too.

Relative to RFC 8446, the document is described as a minor update. Its listed technical changes include forbidding reuse of KeyShare values between connections, forbidding negotiation of TLS 1.0 and 1.1 (deprecated by RFC 8996), clarifying which hash is used with PSKs and HelloRetryRequest, upgrading the requirement to start a key update before exceeding key usage limits to MUST, limiting the number of KeyUpdate messages, and adding a general_error alert. It also drops the word "master" for secrets in favor of "main".

The document also changes a few things for TLS 1.2: a downgrade protection mechanism, RSASSA-PSS signature schemes, and use of the supported_versions extension in preference to legacy_version are all available to 1.2 implementations.

The key derivation labels still use the string "master" (for example "e exp master") even though the values are now called "main" secrets. The RFC says this mismatch exists to retain compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 redesigned TLS 1.2. Every remaining cipher is an AEAD cipher (one that encrypts and authenticates together), and all key exchanges give forward secrecy. All handshake messages after the ServerHello are encrypted, and key derivation now uses HKDF. Compression and DSA were removed. RFC 9846 is a minor update of RFC 8446. It forbids negotiating TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and tightens key update rules.

sections.title: The Handshake
sections.content:
A full handshake takes one round trip before the client can send application data. The client sends a ClientHello carrying a 32-byte random value, a list of cipher suites, and extensions such as key_share, signature_algorithms and supported_versions. The server answers with a ServerHello that picks a single cipher suite and includes its own key_share. From that point both sides can compute shared keys, and everything else is encrypted.

The server then sends EncryptedExtensions, optionally a CertificateRequest, its Certificate and CertificateVerify (a signature over the handshake), and finally Finished, a MAC over the whole handshake. The client replies with its own Finished, preceded by Certificate and CertificateVerify if the server asked for them. The RFC groups this into three phases: Key Exchange, Server Parameters and Authentication.

If the client guessed the wrong key-exchange group, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest, which is a ServerHello whose random field is set to the SHA-256 hash of the string "HelloRetryRequest". The client then sends a second ClientHello with a share for the group the server wants. This costs an extra round trip, and the transcript hash covers both rounds.

A message that arrives out of order is fatal: the receiver must abort with an unexpected_message alert.
sections.plainLanguage: A full handshake takes one round trip before the client can send application data. The client sends a ClientHello with a random value, cipher suites and extensions such as key_share. The server replies with a ServerHello choosing one cipher suite. Both can then compute shared keys, and everything else is encrypted. The server sends its Certificate, a signature (CertificateVerify) and a Finished message, and the client answers with its own Finished.

sections.title: Resumption and 0-RTT
sections.content:
After a handshake completes, the server can send a NewSessionTicket message. It carries a ticket and a lifetime, and the client can present it in a later connection as a pre-shared key (PSK). Servers must not use a lifetime above 604800 seconds (7 days), and clients must not use a ticket for longer than 7 days after issuance. If the server accepts the PSK, the new handshake skips the Certificate and CertificateVerify messages. A client that offers resumption should also send a key_share so the server can fall back to a full handshake. This single mechanism replaces both session IDs and the session tickets of RFC 5077.

With a PSK the client may also send 0-RTT early data in its very first flight, encrypted under a key derived from the PSK. This saves a round trip but costs security: the RFC says TLS provides no inherent replay protection for 0-RTT data, and the early data does not have forward secrecy. Servers should limit replays, for example by single-use tickets, recording ClientHellos, or freshness checks (Section 8), and clients must only send early data that is safe to replay. Early data is not permitted after a HelloRetryRequest.

Do not put a request that changes state (like a payment) in 0-RTT data unless the server is known to prevent replays. An attacker can resend a recorded first flight.
sections.plainLanguage: After a handshake, a server can send a NewSessionTicket that the client presents later as a pre-shared key (PSK). If the server accepts it, the new handshake skips the certificate messages. Tickets last at most 7 days. With a PSK, the client may also send 0-RTT early data in its first flight. This saves a round trip, but TLS gives that data no replay protection or forward secrecy.

sections.title: The Record Protocol
sections.content:
All TLS data travels in records. Each record is at most 2^14 bytes of plaintext, and its header has a content type (handshake is 22, alert is 21, application_data is 23, change_cipher_spec is 20), a legacy version and a 16-bit length. Once keys are in place, every record is protected with an AEAD cipher. The outer header of a protected record always says application_data (23) and version 0x0303; the real content type is hidden inside the encrypted body, optionally followed by zero padding that senders may add to hide lengths.

The ciphertext length may not exceed 2^14 + 256 bytes, and a receiver that sees a record larger than allowed must terminate with a record_overflow alert. The per-record nonce is formed from the record sequence number and an IV derived from the handshake, and the record header serves as the additional authenticated data.

AEAD keys wear out. For AES-GCM, the RFC says about 2^24.5 full-size records (roughly 24 million) can be encrypted under one set of keys, and implementations must either close the connection or do a key update before reaching the limit. For ChaCha20/Poly1305 the sequence number would wrap before the safety limit is reached.
sections.plainLanguage: All TLS data travels in records of at most 2^14 bytes of plaintext. Once keys are in place, every record is protected with an AEAD cipher. The outer header of a protected record always says application_data, and the real content type is hidden inside the encrypted body, which may include padding to hide lengths. AEAD keys wear out, so the RFC limits how many records one key may protect.

sections.title: Keys and Updates
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 derives all of its keys with HKDF. The key schedule starts from a zero-valued input, adds the PSK (if any) to make the Early Secret, then adds the (EC)DHE shared secret to make the Handshake Secret, and finally mixes in zeros to get the Main Secret. At each stage Derive-Secret produces traffic secrets bound to a transcript hash, a hash of the handshake messages so far. Because a transcript hash covers the messages, any tampering with the negotiation changes every key afterward. The hash is the one named by the cipher suite.

Once the handshake is done, either side can send a KeyUpdate message to switch to a fresh set of traffic keys without a new handshake. Both sender and receiver must encrypt the KeyUpdate itself under the old keys. Senders must not allow the number of key updates to exceed 2^48-1.

The same schedule also supports exporters, which let an application derive extra keying material from the connection. RFC 9846 updates RFC 5705 so that exporters no longer distinguish between no context and an empty context.

Early Secret
Built from the PSK; yields the binder key and the client early traffic secret for 0-RTT.
Handshake Secret
Built by adding the (EC)DHE shared secret; protects the handshake messages.
Main Secret
Final stage; yields the application traffic secrets and the resumption secret.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 derives all keys with HKDF. The key schedule mixes in the PSK (if any), then the shared secret from the key exchange, producing traffic secrets bound to a transcript hash, a hash of the handshake so far. Tampering with the negotiation therefore changes every later key. Either side can send a KeyUpdate message to switch to fresh traffic keys without a new handshake.

sections.title: Alerts and What Must Be Implemented
sections.content:
Problems are reported with alerts, each a two-byte structure of a level and a description. In TLS 1.3 the level is mostly ignorable because the kind of alert implies how serious it is. close_notify signals an orderly end of one direction and each side must send it before closing its write side, which protects against truncation. Parse failures use decode_error, and well-formed but invalid values use illegal_parameter. Other examples are handshake_failure (40), bad_certificate (42), protocol_version (70) and the new general_error (117).

For interoperability, a TLS-compliant application must, absent an application profile saying otherwise, implement the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher suite and should implement TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256. It must also support signatures with rsa_pkcs1_sha256 (for certificates), rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 and ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256, and key exchange with secp256r1, while X25519 is a SHOULD. A set of extensions is mandatory, including supported_versions, cookie, signature_algorithms, supported_groups, key_share and server_name.
sections.plainLanguage: Problems are reported with alerts. close_notify signals an orderly end of one direction, and each side must send it before closing, which protects against truncation. Other alerts include decode_error and handshake_failure. For interoperability, an application must implement the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher suite unless its profile says otherwise. It must also support certain signature algorithms and the secp256r1 key exchange.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to its Appendix F for an overview of the intended security properties. The handshake is built so that an active attacker should not be able to force the peers into weaker parameters than they would pick without the attacker. Downgrade is also handled directly: a server that negotiates TLS 1.2 or below overwrites the last 8 bytes of its ServerHello random with a fixed marker, so a TLS 1.3-capable client can notice that it has been pushed down.

Several limits are called out. TLS does not hide message lengths, though padding helps. 0-RTT data can be replayed and lacks forward secrecy. A PSK derived from a low-entropy password is exposed to dictionary attacks via the PSK binder, because the PSK mechanism is explicitly not a password-authenticated key exchange. Appendix F also discusses side-channel attacks, PSK identity exposure, and misbinding when self-signed certificates or raw public keys are used.

The document is clear that TLS 1.3 is not a drop-in cure for everything: how an application checks the identity in a certificate is left to that application, with RFC 9525 cited as useful guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake is built so an active attacker cannot force the peers into weaker parameters. A server that negotiates TLS 1.2 or below marks the end of its ServerHello random, so a TLS 1.3-capable client can detect a downgrade. Limits remain. TLS does not hide message lengths, 0-RTT data can be replayed, and a PSK derived from a low-entropy password is exposed to dictionary attacks.

items.title: Forward secrecy by default
items.text: Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman suites were removed, so public-key key exchanges give forward secrecy.

items.title: Transcript binding
items.text: Keys and Finished messages depend on a hash of the handshake, so tampering with negotiation breaks the connection.

items.title: Key separation
items.text: HKDF with labeled contexts yields independent early, handshake and application secrets.

items.title: Rekeying
items.text: KeyUpdate refreshes traffic keys mid-connection without a new handshake.
